goal: Let the user close out a planned leg by hand from the flight detail page when the flight was linked to that leg manually and has already ended — the case FlightManager.endFlight() can never reach, because the flight was over before the link existed. Marking it flown records arrival_deviation_nm measured from the flight's own arrival position to the planned destination, so the leg reads 'flown, N nm from plan' exactly as an auto-closed leg does; the same control reverses the change, clearing the deviation, without unlinking the flight. Everything outside that gate — auto-linked legs, flights still in the air, unlinked legs — keeps design.md §15's existing behaviour, including the PlannedLegHasLinkedFlightError 409 that finding F-1 introduced.
frozen_decisions: PLACEMENT: flight detail page only — the Planned Leg section of /flight/:id. NOT the trip page leg row. No TripDetail.tsx work is planned.

DEVIATION: compute arrival_deviation_nm from the linked flight's own arrival position against the planned destination (same haversine as recordArrivalOnPlannedLeg), store it, and ALWAYS set the status the user asked for. A hand-mark beyond ARRIVAL_RADIUS_NM is still 'flown', never 'diverted'. The touchdown rule is deliberately not mirrored.
REVERSIBLE: the same control toggles a hand-marked leg back to 'planned', clearing arrival_deviation_nm, WITHOUT unlinking the flight.

No test framework. Verification is npx tsc --noEmit, curl against a scratch server on a non-3000 port against a COPY of the database, better-sqlite3 queries under Node 20, and a ts-node CLI inspector.
Sub-agents do not commit, push, or switch branches.
sequencing_rationale: Design is its own task and blocks everything, because the run turns on one contested decision — how far to narrow F-1 — and the live database has evidence on both sides of it: flight 56 → leg 12 is the stuck case the user is asking about, while flights 47 → leg 4 and 52 → leg 10 are manual links whose legs the SYSTEM closed at touchdown. A gate keyed only on 'manual' hands the user a control that can clear a real touchdown measurement. That has to be settled in prose before any of it is typed.

The Orchestrator's proposed gate looks survivable and the plan is built for it, but the Designer must confirm rather than inherit it: closeFlight() (src/db.ts:321) stores exactly the frame endFlight() measures the deviation from, so recomputing from flights.arrival_lat/lon reproduces the stored value — a read-only check over all 8 linked pairs in the live database agreed on 7/7 closed legs. If that holds, nothing a hand-reverse clears is unrecoverable, which is what makes the narrowing safe. T-001 must reproduce that result itself; if it fails, the design returns blocked instead of guessing.

The genuinely risky logic — who may close a leg, and how far off plan they landed — is a pure function of four columns, so it goes in src/plannedLegClose.ts with no ./db import and its own inspector (T-002). That is what makes it falsifiable with no sim, no browser and no test framework, which is the only kind of verification this repo has.

T-002 (new files) and T-003 (src/db.ts) run in parallel on disjoint paths. That is only safe because T-001 is required to place the composition in the endpoint, so src/db.ts never imports src/plannedLegClose.ts — the file-ownership decision is made in the design, not discovered during implementation.

T-004 lands the endpoint alone, after both, because the endpoint is where an F-1 regression would actually appear, and its acceptance is differential: the same four PATCH requests fired at a server built from `git archive HEAD` and at the new one, byte-for-byte identical.

The escape hatch is not deferred to a later phase: the reverse transition (flown → planned, link kept) is specified, implemented and tested in the same tasks as the forward one. A mark-flown the user cannot undo leaves Unlink as the only repair — and Unlink is the destructive operation this whole feature exists to avoid.

Phase 1 ships without a single line of client code, because plannedLegBadge() and plannedLegLandingNote() already speak 'flown' and 'flown, N nm from plan' for every consumer. The seam between phase 1 and phase 2 is therefore the seam between 'the record is right' and 'the user can fix it without curl' — both visible, in that order.
README ships with the UI, not after it, because README's linking table currently tells the user that landing is the only route to 'flown'.

The build is its own phase and runs last because `npm run build:client` publishes the UI to the user's already-running server the instant it completes, with no restart — while the endpoint it calls does not exist until the user restarts. That window is not a bug to fix, it is a fact to state, and it belongs at the end where it is shortest.

Every phase ends in a Reviewer that re-runs the evidence, and each phase's first task depends on the previous phase's Reviewer, so no two tasks touching src/server.ts or the client ever run concurrently.

phases.name: The API can close a hand-linked leg
phases.ships: Through the API (verified on a copy of the database), the stuck case in the user's own logbook — flight 56, hand-linked to leg 12, PAJN, ended, still reading 'Planned' — can be marked flown with its real 0.3 nm deviation recorded, and marked back to planned again without unlinking. Because plannedLegBadge() and plannedLegLandingNote() already render 'flown' and 'flown, N nm from plan', the trip page and the flight page read correctly the moment the row changes, with no client code at all.

phases.name: The button
phases.ships: The user can do it without curl: a control in the Planned Leg section of /flight/:id marks the leg flown and marks it back, absent on auto-linked flights and on flights still in the air, and README describes it where manual linking is already described.

phases.name: Ship
phases.ships: Built artifacts the user's next restart picks up, smoke-tested on a copy, with the build-to-restart window stated explicitly so the user is not surprised by a button that 404s until they restart.

tasks.title: Freeze the gate, the deviation rule, the API surface and the module split; amend the prior design in place
tasks.goal: Settle the one genuinely contested decision in this run — how far design.md §15's F-1 rule ('a linked leg's status is not the user's to set at all') is narrowed — and freeze every contract the four implementation tasks then execute without a second judgement call.
acceptance_criteria: design.md §1 'The gate' states the eligibility predicate for BOTH directions (→flown, →planned) as a single boolean expression over named columns (flights.planned_leg_link_source, flights.end_time, flights.planned_leg_id, planned_legs.status), and backs it with a table that has one row for every combination of link source {auto, manual, null} × flight {ended, in air} × leg status {planned, flown, diverted, skipped} — 24 rows, no gaps, no 'etc.' — each marked allow→flown / allow→planned / refuse-with-<http status>. T-002's inspector is written straight off this table, so a missing row is a missing test.

It resolves the system-closed manual link explicitly, by name. The live database contains two: flight 47 → leg 4 (arrival_deviation_nm 0.4, KSFO) and flight 52 → leg 10 (0.8, CYVR) are planned_leg_link_source='manual' whose legs were closed by endFlight() at touchdown, not by hand. Under the Orchestrator's proposed gate (manual AND ended) these become user-reversible and their touchdown-measured deviation clearable. The section states whether that is accepted and why, or how it is excluded. If exclusion needs a new column, or the choice is one only the user can make, the task returns status 'blocked' with that question rather than choosing.

tasks.title: src/server.ts — the endpoint, the gate composition, and proof the old PATCH contract did not move
tasks.goal: Wire the pure module and the writer into the HTTP surface design.md §'API' froze, and demonstrate by differential test that every request the server answered before this run still gets the same answer.
acceptance_criteria: The endpoint is exactly the method, path, body and payload of design.md §'API', composing src/plannedLegClose.ts for eligibility and deviation and src/db.ts for the write; `export NVM_DIR="$HOME/.nvm"; . "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh"; nvm use 20; npx tsc --noEmit` exits 0.

A scratch server answers on port 3100 with its cwd set to a scratch directory holding a COPY of the database, so that src/db.ts:9's `path.join(process.cwd(),'flights.db')` and src/server.ts:106's static root both resolve inside the scratch tree and cannot reach the live file. The report states the exact commands used to start and to stop it, and `ss -ltn | grep 3100` prints nothing at the end.

A curl matrix, one row per case, each showing the observed status code and body: (a) flight 56 → 200, leg 12 reads status 'flown', arrival_deviation_nm 0.3; (b) the reverse → 200, status 'planned', deviation null, and GET /api/flights/56 still shows planned_leg_id 12 and planned_leg_link_source 'manual'; (c) flight 48 (auto link) → 409; (d) a flight with end_time NULL (created in the copy) → 409; (e) a flight with no planned_leg_id → the code design.md §'API' specifies; (f) unknown flight id → 404; non-numeric id → 400; body without a valid status → 400.

The F-1 regression is proved differentially, not by assertion: the pre-change server is materialised with `git archive HEAD | tar -x -C $S/base` (no branch switch, no worktree, no stash), run on port 3101 against an identical copy of the same scratch database, and these four requests are sent to BOTH servers — PATCH /api/planned-legs/<unlinked leg> {status:'skipped'}, {status:'planned'}, {status:'flown'}, and PATCH on linked leg 12 — with the report showing the status code and body from each, pairwise identical.

Route registration order is respected: any new literal path segment is registered before the /:id routes and before the SPA catch-all (prior design.md §7.3); the report shows the new route reached with a 4xx/200 rather than the SPA's index.html.
`md5sum flights.db` identical before and after; both values in the report. `git status --porcelain` lists only src/server.ts and the report.
risks: This endpoint is the whole security boundary of the feature: everything the gate refuses, it refuses here.

global_risks: The system-closed manual link. Live rows flight 47 → leg 4 (0.4 nm) and flight 52 → leg 10 (0.8 nm) are manual links whose legs endFlight() closed at touchdown. Under a 'manual AND ended' gate, the user can reopen them and clear a measurement the system took. Mitigated by the recompute being exact (7/7 in a read-only check), so nothing is lost that cannot be recreated — but T-001 owns the decision, and if it wants those excluded it needs a new column, which turns a no-migration run into a migration. RANKED FIRST because it is the only thing that can change the shape of the plan.

Predicate drift between client and server. The client cannot import src/, so the button's visibility rule is a hand-copy of the server gate. Nothing in the build links them. Mitigated by freezing one predicate in design.md §'UI' and making T-008 diff both against all 24 gate rows; unmitigated in the long run.

Regressing F-1. Widening any path that reaches setPlannedLegStatus() risks restoring exactly the bug the previous run's review had to fix: PATCH {status:'planned'} on a linked flown leg returning 200 and destroying arrival_deviation_nm. Mitigated by the differential test against `git archive HEAD` and by forbidding any diff inside that function.

The build-to-restart window. `npm run build:client` writes client/dist, which src/server.ts:106 serves statically from the LIVE process — the new button appears to the user immediately, while the endpoint behind it only exists after they restart node dist/index.js. Mitigated only by T-009 stating it and the Orchestrator relaying it.

Unexercised NULL-arrival path. Zero flights in the live database have end_time set and arrival_lat NULL, so the 'cannot measure a deviation' branch has no real data behind it and only the inspector's synthetic row will ever have run it.

Rounding divergence. If the hand path rounds differently from src/flightManager.ts:463, the same flight reads a different deviation depending on which path closed the leg. Mitigated by an inspector row that fails if the two expressions differ.

Scope creep toward the trip page. The trip page shows the same legs and the same badges, and 'why not here too' is one line of JSX away. Frozen decision 1 says no; TripDetail.tsx appears in no task's allowed_paths.
open_questions: Is a 'diverted' leg reversible by hand? The frozen decisions cover flown ↔ planned only. T-001 must fill the cell rather than leave the endpoint's behaviour to fall out of the code.
What happens when the leg is 'skipped' AND hand-linked — a combination the previous design calls contradictory and refuses with a 409? T-001 says whether this feature changes that answer.

Flight-scoped route (PUT /api/flights/:id/planned-leg-status) or a widened PATCH /api/planned-legs/:legId? The flight-scoped shape expresses the gate's own subject and leaves the leg endpoint untouched, but T-001 owns the choice and must state the reason.
model_policy: opus for the design freeze, the endpoint and every review — contested judgement, the trust boundary, and adversarial re-execution. sonnet for the scoped implementation tasks whose contracts are already frozen. haiku for the README edit, which is two named regions of one file. Any task that returns blocked is re-issued at opus.
